The pages provided do not contain Boeing's FY2022 income statement or gross margin figures (revenue and cost of sales), so an FY2022 gross margin trend cannot be computed from them. The only relevant Boeing content is the FY2018 10-K, which indicates gross margin is of limited use as a trend metric for Boeing: it uses program accounting, where cost of sales is set by applying an estimated cost-of-sales percentage across the whole program accounting quantity. New programs like the 787 and 777X carry lower initial margins and deferred production costs, and reach-forward losses (e.g., $1,258 million on the 747 in 2016) are booked immediately. Changes in estimates can therefore swing reported margins. A 1% change in estimated gross margin on long-term contracts moved 2018 pre-tax income by about $297 million. Reported gross margin therefore reflects accounting estimates and program timing as much as underlying operating improvement. Whether it improved in FY2022 cannot be determined from these pages.
